sentences.text: Choice screens are not market choice

A choice screen can look like freedom while functioning as a velvet rope. You see a row of options, you click one, and the interface congratulates you for exercising power that somebody else has already bounded.
Who chose the row? Not you.

The gatekeeper did – the platform that controls the screen, the marketplace that controls the shelf, the operating system that controls the prompt. It decides which options qualify for admission, which ones appear first, which ones are buried under a secondary menu, and which ones never get shown at all (but I repeat myself).
That first act is easy to miss because the screen presents selection as the whole event. It isn't.

Selection starts earlier, with the power to compose the menu. If we can choose only among the things a gatekeeper has selected, then our choice is real in the narrow sense and managed in the larger one.

A restaurant can offer you twelve dishes, but the number twelve tells you nothing about who decided what counts as food. A software prompt can offer six browsers, payment services, or search providers, but the list itself is already an argument about which futures deserve to be visible.
The menu is not the market. The menu is the gate.

Then there are defaults – the options that arrive preselected, preinstalled, or placed beneath the cursor. You can change them, of course, if you notice them, understand them, have the time to investigate them, and can tolerate the friction attached to refusing the recommendation.
That isn't a small qualification; it's the operating theory. Most people don't approach every setting as a constitutional convention, drafting amendments before they click Continue.

We use what arrives ready to use because attention is scarce and because the cost of making a different choice is often hidden in the interface itself. A default turns the path of least resistance into the path that looks normal.
What happens when the supposedly neutral screen gives one option a bright button and the others a grey link? What happens when refusal requires three screens and acceptance requires one?
The answer isn't mysterious. The design has converted convenience into conduct.

A default doesn't need to force you in order to shape what you'll do; it only needs to make one action easier to see, easier to understand, or easier to finish. That is power with a user-friendly face.
And naturally, the gatekeeper can call this arrangement choice. The word does useful work: it moves attention away from the person who designed the corridor and toward the person walking through it.

This is how nominal choice preserves gatekeeper power. The gatekeeper keeps control over entry, ordering, eligibility, visibility, and the terms of switching, while we receive the ceremonial privilege of picking from the approved tray.
You can choose the lock's colour while somebody else keeps the key.

Even a crowded screen can preserve that arrangement. More buttons don't necessarily mean more power for you; they may simply make the gate harder to see (a little camouflage, a little bullshit, and the same old ownership).
If every road begins at the same tollbooth, adding signposts doesn't make the tollbooth disappear.
A meaningful remedy would change the structure, not merely decorate the prompt.

It would require the gatekeeper to explain who selected the options, what criteria govern admission, how ordering works, and what the default actually does. Those explanations would have to be intelligible before the click, not buried in a document you won't read because the product is holding your work hostage.
It would make every option genuinely reachable, with refusal no harder than acceptance and switching no harder than staying put.
It would also let independent providers reach the user on fair terms, rather than asking them to beg for a place on the one screen that matters.

Most importantly, the remedy would move power over the menu. You wouldn't merely choose an item from somebody else's tray; you could bring another item to the table, inspect the rules that govern the table, and leave for a different table without losing the meal.
That sounds less tidy, and it may create more decisions. Good.

A market is not meaningful because a screen contains alternatives. It is meaningful when people can enter, compare, switch, and offer alternatives without asking the incumbent gatekeeper for permission.
Choice after curation is still choice, but it isn't market choice.
